How this is organised

AI's default failure mode is being reached for on every problem, whether or not it's the right tool. That's how systems get expensive, wrong, and hard to trust. Both tasks here put the deterministic path first, and bring the model in only where real inference is needed, with guardrails around it.

Intro

Both of these are built with AI, and both use very little of it. Inside each system the model is invoked exactly where inference is needed. That keeps cost down, but the bigger reason is standards: what should be deterministic stays deterministic, and AI's judgement gets spent only where it earns its place.

Task 1 reduces a messy record to a handful of decisions, and the model only touches the ones left over. Task 2 is architected to reduce millions of session and integration logs into a curated dataset of a few hundred to a few thousand rows, and the model only writes the sentences. In this build's mock data flow, that's roughly two million events collapsed to 496 published rows.

Most of the system is data cleaning and reduction. AI gets brought in only when inference is actually needed.

The two builds land on the same shape, at very different scales:

PropertyTask 1, enrichmentTask 2, QBR insight
Reduce before the modelTwo gates cut the work before any provider or model runsMillions of events become a few hundred published rows before any prompt exists, mock build: 2,068,975 → 496
The model gets a closed setMaps a value onto a fixed vocabulary, or declinesPicks one section id from a registry, then writes prose
Everything is checkedA quality gate on every value before it's acceptedEvery figure in the prose is re-checked against the data behind it
The model's share shrinksLearned map: 5 calls, then 1, then 0Every new section is one more thing selected, not computed

Claude, through Claude Code, wrote most of the implementation in both tasks from designs I specified and reviewed. The architecture, the decisions and the tradeoffs are mine. My Python is AI-augmented; my SQL and data modelling are not, and that's the half that carries the load here.

Part one

Task 1

Lead-record enrichment.

Task 1 · Why AI is almost not needed

A wrong field costs more than a missing one.

Accounts arrive from many sources with holes in them. Firing every data provider at every record and letting the model tidy up whatever comes back is expensive, unauditable, and it degrades good data: a confidently wrong headcount overwrites a correct blank.

$0.60
provider-lookup cost per account (illustrative, blended)
$0.001
model cost per account

At this ratio, model cost stops being a lever. The lever that remains is accuracy, in the few places the model is actually used.

Task 1 · Decision gates

Two gates, and a four-way verdict.

Gate A, before anything runs

Does this field need enriching at all?

What Gate A checks
  • Is the account enrichable at all: a business domain, a company name, or a person to resolve against?
  • Is the field on the funnel-agreed list of fields that move a deal forward, or one the user has chosen to enrich?
  • Is it genuinely missing, which includes present-but-useless, like a personal address where a corporate one is needed?

Roughly 30% of work never happens, before any provider is called or any model runs.

Gate B, after a value returns

Is this value good enough to keep?

Checks format, provider confidence, consistency, and plausibility, then routes the result to one of the four outcomes below: keep it, retry with another provider, drop it, or send it for reconciliation.

The four-way verdict
accept, keep the value recoverable, try the next provider hard fail, drop and never retry vocabulary mismatch, reconcile with AI

A third deterministic step sits between them.

Which provider gets called is its own fixed lookup: one primary source per field, and a provider is called only when it owns at least one field that is still missing. Never every provider at once.

The two-outcome version of Gate B is the obvious one, and it's quietly wrong. It either waterfalls on data that was already correct, or it accepts an implausible number on a second guess.

Task 1 · Where AI is actually involved

One outcome out of four calls the model.

A vocabulary mismatch: the value is valid, and nothing in the deterministic map covers it yet. An unknown country token, a platform alias, a job title that was never seeded. That is the whole of the model's job here.

A model proposal only becomes a permanent mapping once reviewers agree, and from that moment the deterministic lookup catches it, for every account, until we decide otherwise.

What the model is told
  • Its role: the reconciliation step in the enrichment pipeline, and the end goal it serves, feeding the CRM clean contact data.
  • When it is being called: only after the value already passed format validation and missed every seeded alias and confirmed mapping.
  • Its job: pick exactly one canonical term from a fixed allowed list, or say none fit. Nothing outside that list is a valid answer.
  • What happens to its answer: it is a proposal, not a final decision, held behind human review before it can become a permanent mapping.

The model's output enters through a review gate, and its share of the work is a number that trends down and is visible on a dashboard.

Task 1 · Architecture of the solution

One step in ten is the model, and it writes itself out of the loop.

The mapped terms table is the seeded plus previously-confirmed vocabulary for every reconciled field. It is checked first, before the model is ever asked. Only a value nobody has confirmed a mapping for reaches the model.

Task 1 · Live demo

Model calls per run, across three runs. The system learns its own vocabulary and stops needing the model.

talon-one-task1.onrender.com

  1. Load the demo list. Watch the badge on each field, deterministic or model. Five fields need the model on this run.
  2. Write to CRM. This is the step that matters: it promotes each confirmed proposal into the deterministic map. A proposal is never cached on its own.

Explore freely. The presentation demo starts by resetting the learned map, so anything you try beforehand washes out.

Part two

Task 2

QBR insight pipeline.

Task 2 · QBR insight pipeline

How to plug AI onto data properly.

Three ways to get a quarterly business review out of a few million session events. Two of them break, for different reasons, and the reasons are what shape the third.

Option one
AI reads the raw event stream

1.25 billion tokens for one account for one month. That exceeds any context window on the market, at any price, and chunking does not close a gap of that size.

Option two
AI writes the SQL

Metric definitions drift between prompts, the tenant boundary depends on the model behaving, and every request opens a new injection surface.

What this build does
Curate, map to semantics, AI queries.

A dbt DAG collapses raw events into a small published layer. A semantic layer sits on top of it, and that layer is the only thing AI ever touches. It picks a bundle id from a fixed set.

Task 2 · Why AI is almost not needed

Option one is arithmetic, not opinion.

One mid-size account, one month, is about 5 GB of session and integration logs.

1.25B
tokens, roughly
1,250×
a 1M-token context window
$3,750
per account, per month, if it fit

It doesn't fit. Chunking leaves a 1,250× gap, and so does next year's context window. The reduction is the system, and everything after this is consequence.

Task 2 · Architecture of the solution

We have the curated data. Why not let the model query it?

Once the reduction has run, the data is small, clean and published. The obvious next move is to hand the model a connection and let it write its own SQL. That is option two, and three things break at that point.

  • Metric definitions drift. Redemption rate computed one way in one prompt and another way in the next, with no single place that settles it.
  • The tenant boundary depends on the model behaving. A filter the model is asked to include is a filter the model can omit.
  • Every request is a new injection surface. Free text reaching a query planner is the whole attack, and prompt engineering addresses none of the three.

Removing the model's ability to write a query addresses all three at once. A semantic layer takes the query away and accepts a bundle id instead.

Task 2 · Why the third path works

A DAG shrinks the data. A semantic layer locks down what a question means.

The DAG

A fixed sequence of steps, each one throwing away what nothing downstream needs

A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is just an ordered pipeline: step two can't start until step one finishes, and nothing runs twice. Each step here either reshapes the data or drops rows and columns nobody downstream needs. What comes out isn't a copy of the events, it's a curated summary of them.

The semantic layer

Every metric gets one name and one definition, decided once

It sits on top of the curated data and publishes a fixed catalogue: "redemption rate," "active coupons," each backed by exactly one query. Nobody, human or model, writes their own version of that math. They pick the name; the layer already knows the SQL.

Together they do the job an LLM was about to be asked to do badly: the DAG decides what's worth keeping, the semantic layer decides what a question even means. Both are settled before AI is ever involved.

Task 2 · How one answer actually happens

The model never sees a number it didn't ask a fixed question for.

  1. AI picks a question. Not free text: one id from the fixed catalogue the semantic layer publishes, like redemption_rate_by_segment.
  2. The semantic layer resolves it. That id maps to one pre-declared query, with the tenant filter already attached from the caller's token.
  3. The warehouse returns a number. A rate, a count, a delta. No prose, no interpretation, just the figure.
  4. AI wraps it in a sentence. The only thing generated freely is the English around a number that was already computed and already correct.

Swap the order and it breaks: a model that writes the query first can get the query wrong. Here it can only ever be wrong about the sentence, and even that gets checked against the number before anyone sees it.

Task 2 · Architecture of the solution

Two pieces do the work the model is kept away from.

There is no code path from free text into a query.

The model picks a bundle id. Python resolves that bundle's pre-declared query, qualifies its member names against the bundle's own declared view, and substitutes only the placeholders it already knows, quarter and prior_quarter. An unknown placeholder raises.

Task 2 · Architecture of the solution

21 models, four layers, one direction.

The DAG carries its own tests, built to catch quirks like these.

67 tests run on every build. Some check a single field, like a value never being null or always falling in a known range. Others check across tables, so two tables can't quietly disagree on the same number, one saying $40K in sales, the other $42K. Five of the cross-table checks carry real weight:

  • No PII in the published layer. Fails the build if a personal or session identifier reaches rpt_.
  • The reduction ratio holds. The funnel below is enforced by CI, not asserted in a document.
  • Period-over-period reconciles. Recomputed independently, so a silently wrong "down 22% on last quarter" fails rather than reads plausibly.
  • Coupon facts don't fan out. A reintroduced join would double counts while leaving the rate correct, which is the quiet kind of wrong.
  • No orphan effects. A broken lineage join would corrupt every per-segment number in the pack.
Task 2 · Architecture of the solution

In this build's mock data: 2,068,975 events, down to 496 published rows.

StageVolumeCumulative reduction
Raw events2,068,975 (~380 MB)1×
Typed and deduplicatedsame rows1×
Lineage layerno reduction, deliberately1×
Daily fact grain49,523 rows42×
Published reporting rows496 rows, 48 KB4,171×
Payload handed to the modela few thousand tokens~46,000×

Row counts are measured from a real run of this build's pipeline against generated data, not from Talon.One's own systems. The token figure is an estimate, and I'd rather say which is which than present both the same way.

Redemption rate is stored as its components, never as a saved ratio. Averaging a rate across grains produces an answer that is wrong and still looks plausible, so a dedicated test fails the build if a join ever re-inflates the coupon counts.

Task 2 · Architecture of the solution

What feeds /create-qbr.

Two inputs, built independently, meeting at one point. The warehouse says what moved. The account record says why.

Task 2 · Where AI is actually involved

The boundary is enforced below the model, where it can't be argued with.

The model picks a section id and writes sentences. Everything that decides what data it is allowed to see happens underneath it, in code it never touches.

Every underlying table is private, and only curated views are queryable. A tenant filter is appended from the caller's signed token before the request is planned, so it was never part of the request that was submitted, and there is nothing for a caller to opt out of.

Four cases run as tests against a live semantic layer on every build: an account reads its own metrics, a private table is refused, one account asking for another's data returns zero rows, and a token with no tenant claim is rejected outright. This is a demonstrated property, not a claim in a design document.

Task 2 · Where this goes

Self-serve data, starting with the QBR.

The two hard parts of self-serve data are already built and already tested: a tenant boundary that holds under adversarial cases, and a catalogue of metrics that can't be gotten wrong. Right now that catalogue is small and the questions are fixed, one per QBR section.

Cube's own schema validation extends to a much richer case: a model composing measures and dimensions freely from plain language, still checked against the same declared catalogue before it can run. Opening that up is the natural next step, not a rebuild.

The QBR is one consumer of that catalogue. A Slack bot, an account health dashboard, a rep's own question before a call, none of them need new trust built, because the trust was built once, at the semantic layer.

Task 2 · Ranking

Salience decides what deserves the customer's time.

Statistics can tell you a number moved unusually. They have no opinion on whether anyone should care. Salience is the score that answers the second question: impact times confidence, with ease left out on purpose, because how hard something is to fix has no bearing on whether the account deserves to hear about it.

Surfaced · score 0.36
Winback campaign redemption rate collapses, around 21% fall
z = −4.06
significance
Suppressed · score 0.024
Coupon rejection volume rising
z = +3.55
significance

Near-identical significance. Opposite decisions. A fifteenfold gap, produced entirely by two numbers a human chose and can change.

Detection is deterministic SQL. The materiality ranking is business logic sitting outside the warehouse, in forty readable lines, where it can be retuned without a rebuild. If RevOps thinks reliability should outrank discount volume, that is a conversation about one constant.

Task 2 · Retrieval

A folder of files becomes the context the model writes from.

Each account has a small corpus: call transcripts, CRM notes, support cases, logged commitments, one file per document. Every file carries the same frontmatter, so retrieval never has to guess what a document is or who it belongs to.

Context explains a number. It never produces one.

A QBR is a conversation, not a numbers dump. Why redemption fell lives in a sales call or an account note, never in a fact table. Retrieval is driven by the anomalies salience already surfaced, and every passage is cited alongside them.

Retrieved · cited [C1]
Gong call, 2026-06-18: the account's own head of CRM says they narrowed the winback audience themselves in April, and expected exactly this fall.
Filtered · visibility: internal
Salesforce note, same account, same entity tag: renewal pricing strategy and a competitor mention, marked "do not share with customer." Never reaches the model.

Same entity tag on both documents, and either could have scored well against the same query. One gets cited. The other is filtered before generation, because filtering afterwards is not a control: the model has already read it, and a model cannot unread something.

Task 2 · Demo

/create-qbr

A skill that turns a quarter of warehouse data and an account's own call history into a customer-ready review, with every figure checked before it renders.

What you do

  1. Run /create-qbr.
  2. Answer three questions: account, quarter, focus.
  3. It queries the warehouse, ranks the anomalies, retrieves supporting context, and writes the narrative.
  4. Every figure is checked against its source before anything renders.
  5. One self-contained HTML report comes out the other end.

Behind the command sit two phases. Query and rank run first, and stop. Then the narrative is written, checked against source, and rendered. The check runs on its own afterwards, so it works the same whether a person or a model wrote the prose.

Closing

Built by one person with AI, so the handover has to be written down.

When a team builds something, the context lives in several heads. When one person builds it, the context lives in one head, and it leaves when they do. Whoever picks this up next will probably also be working with AI, and an AI reading a codebase with no map produces a plausible change that breaks an invariant nobody wrote down.

So both submissions ship with the map, including the parts that are wrong, thin, or deliberately unusual.
